# Glossary

## Terms

These definitions follow this library's usage. Theory-dependent meanings are qualified explicitly.

| Term | Meaning and limit |
| --- | --- |
| Motion | Change of position, orientation, or spatial arrangement under specified comparison rules; broader uses are stated separately |
| Change | Nonconstancy of a history under selected equality criteria |
| State | An alternative description of a system in a given context |
| Configuration | A system's arrangement; not always a sufficient complete dynamical state |
| Identity | Criteria for the referent remaining the same system or part |
| Distinction | Meaningful inequality within a stated framework |
| Representational equivalence | Descriptions expressing the same physical state under theoretical rules |
| Equivalence relation | A reflexive, symmetric, transitive relation |
| Quotient space | Equivalence classes with additional structure when specified |
| Coarse-graining | A map retaining partial information and potentially merging distinct states |
| Observable | A theory-defined quantity or measurement structure; not always a pre-existing definite value |
| History | States or configurations related to temporal contexts |
| Geometric path | A traversed trace or curve, distinguished from traversal timing |
| Event | In relativity, a spacetime element, not an entire extended process |
| Partial order | An order not requiring every pair to be comparable |
| Total order | An order requiring pairwise comparability |
| Duration | A temporal interval quantity under a specified structure or procedure |
| Parameter | A history-domain label; not necessarily physical clock time |
| Reparametrization | A change of traversal parameter under specified transformation conditions |
| Coordinate time | The temporal coordinate of a description |
| Proper time | Geometric duration along a timelike curve in relativity |
| Simultaneity | Events having the same time under a selected structure |
| Causality | Possible influence according to a theory; not merely list order |
| Position | A place in a space or relative to spatial relations |
| Coordinates | Labels representing points or configurations |
| Physical space | Spatial structure modelled as physical locations or relations |
| Configuration space | The set of configurations considered |
| Phase space | Position–momentum state space in suitable classical formulations |
| Topology | An open-set structure determining, among other things, continuity |
| Distance metric | A positive distance function with identity, symmetry, and the triangle inequality |
| Lorentzian metric | A spacetime bilinear structure with a specified signature; not a positive distance metric |
| Affine structure | Structure permitting point differences without a privileged origin |
| Smooth manifold | A space with compatible local coordinates for differential calculus |
| Reference | A comparison rule or system for relations and changes |
| Inertial frame | A frame with theory-defined free-motion structure |
| Symmetry | A transformation preserving specified structure |
| Invariant | A property or quantity preserved by a stated transformation class |
| Gauge | Theory-defined representational redundancy, not every symmetry |
| Continuity | Preservation of topological proximity through open-set preimages |
| Differentiability | Existence of an appropriate derivative structure |
| Velocity | A position-change vector per time parameter when structure and limits permit |
| Speed | Rate magnitude under a metric or norm, without vector direction |
| Rest | Constant configuration on a stated domain under a specified reference and equality |
| Kinematics | The structure of motion descriptions |
| Dynamics | Laws restricting histories in a theory |
| Stationary | Unchanging in a specified sense: state, distribution, statistics, or quantity |
| Probability current | A quantum-theoretical structure associated with probability conservation, not an individual-trajectory definition |
| Measurand | The quantity intended to be measured |
| Identifiability | Uniqueness of the queried property among data-compatible models or histories |
| Uncertainty | Limits on value determination given information and a measurement model |
| Motion perception | Experience or judgement of motion, distinguished from stimuli and physical inference |

## Notation

| Symbol | Usage |
| --- | --- |
| \(S\) | State space |
| \(Q\) | Configuration space |
| \(T\) | Temporal domain |
| \(s(t),q(t)\) | State or configuration along a history |
| \(x,\mathbf r\) | Spatial location or coordinates, context-dependent |
| \(\sim,[s]\) | Equivalence and equivalence classes |
| \(d\) | Positive distance metric |
| \(g_{\mu\nu}\) | Lorentzian metric components with \((-+++)\) convention |
| \(\lambda\) | General parameter |
| \(\tau\) | Proper time on a timelike curve |
| \(R\) | Rotation matrix or reference name, specified locally |
| \(H,\mathcal O\) | Observation maps; not a Hamiltonian unless stated |
| \(\psi,\rho,j\) | Wavefunction, probability density, probability current |
| \(c,\hbar\) | Vacuum speed of light and reduced Planck constant |

Repeated tensor indices are summed. Examples such as \(q=t^3\) use dimensionless mathematical variables or normalized coordinates; physical quantities require appropriate dimensional factors.

# Motion

A scientific library of motion's foundations and consequences derived by connecting them.

## Two knowledge layers

| Layer | Content | Entry point |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Foundation | State, Time, Space, Reference, Change, Evidence; architecture, sources, initial review | [Foundation/README.md](Foundation/README.md) |
| Synthesis | Cross-foundation reasoning, conditional derivations, counterexamples, unification limits | [Synthesis/Overview.md](Synthesis/Overview.md) |

At the synthesis stage, all 16 Foundation source files were preserved without content changes and moved together into Foundation so their relative links remained valid. Foundation's README and review recorded that initial stage; this index described the pre-Graph project. The repository's English edition translates these documents and records both source and edition identities.

## Synthesis results

The main distinction is between **consistent comparison**, **descriptive sufficiency**, and **evidential sufficiency**. They constrain one another but do not have identical physical meanings.

Several results share a mathematical pattern: a conclusion can be formulated from a limited description when its value agrees across all possibilities merged by that description. This gives conditions for state reduction, consistent transformations, reduced evolution, and data identifiability. Shared form does not prove ontological identity of these questions.

| File | Substance |
| --- | --- |
| [Comparison.md](Synthesis/Comparison.md) | Consistent comparison under coordinate changes; invariance levels; partial orders |
| [Reduction.md](Synthesis/Reduction.md) | When conclusions, transformations, and evolution descend to reduced descriptions |
| [Evidence.md](Synthesis/Evidence.md) | Property identifiability; data-processing limits; geometric bounds with bounded errors |
| [Stationarity.md](Synthesis/Stationarity.md) | Constancy of observables, distributions, currents, and state representations |
| [Limits.md](Synthesis/Limits.md) | Justification types, added premises, contextual incompatibility, open questions |
| [Sources.md](Synthesis/Sources.md) | Foundation sources and additional references |
| [Review.md](Synthesis/Review.md) | Derivation review, counterexamples, refinements of original sources |
| [Trace.tsv](Synthesis/Trace.tsv) | Each result's premises, foundations, arguments, limits |
| [Origins.tsv](Synthesis/Origins.tsv) | Original locations, preserved paths, and source SHA-256 identities |

P01–P13 are trace identifiers, not a count of Motion axioms or claims of new literature discoveries.

## Scientific status

Definitions, conditional theorems, mathematical examples, inherited empirical findings, and conceptual synthesis remain distinct. Mathematical proof alone does not select the physically correct model.

This snapshot is translated into English with standard terminology and notation; filenames and folders are English.

The original **Motion.zip** had one Motion root with separate Foundation and Synthesis. It excluded itself. [Checksums.tsv](Checksums.tsv) covered project content except itself and the archive; Foundation/Checksums.tsv covered the internal Foundation layout. The embedded manifests in this translated snapshot retain that pre-Graph scope.

The synthesis was compiled and checked on **2 November 2026**. This historical snapshot predates machine implementation or Graph integration.

# Comparison

## Comparison precedes constancy claims

Calling configurations at two times “equal” requires a rule connecting those contexts. Equal coordinates alone are insufficient if origins or bases change. Different coordinates do not establish physical change if labels change.

[Reference](../Foundation/Core/Reference.md) presents \(q_t\in Q_t\) and comparison maps \(F_t:Q_t\to Q_R\). [State](../Foundation/Core/State.md) establishes equality's role; [Time](../Foundation/Core/Time.md) distinguishes time from parameters. Together they yield the following consistency condition.

## P01

**Covariance of comparison rules.**

**Premises.** For each \(t\), let \(f_t:Q_t\to Q'_t\) be a representational bijection, \(q_t\) a configuration, and \(F_t\) a comparison rule. All maps apply on the domains considered. Define:

\[
q'_t=f_t(q_t),\qquad F'_t=F_t\circ f_t^{-1}.
\]

**Conclusion.**

\[
F'_t(q'_t)=F_t(q_t).
\]

**Proof.** Substitution gives \(F_t(f_t^{-1}(f_t(q_t)))=F_t(q_t)\). Identical comparison histories at every context preserve constancy, endpoint differences, and other properties of that history.

This is map algebra requiring neither continuity nor differentiability. Preserving those properties in coordinates additionally requires compatible transformations.

**Example.** On a line with shared time, take \(q(t)=t\) and fixed-reference \(F_t(x)=x\). Change coordinates to \(x'=x-t\). The object's coordinates become \(q'(t)=0\), but the same comparison rule becomes \(F'_t(x')=x'+t\). Thus \(F'_t(q'(t))=t\): change relative to the original reference remains.

Using \(G'_t(x')=x'\) after this coordinate change instead selects a different comparison: a reference following the moving origin. Its constant result does not contradict P01 because the physical comparison rule changed.

**Conceptual consequence.** Relative-motion predicates concern the state **together with its reference and comparison rules**, rather than object coordinates alone. This does not make every \(F_t\) family physically realizable or guarantee a global comparison in every spacetime.

## P02

**Preserving a property requires compatible structure.**

Let \(h:T\to Q\), with time-independent \(f:Q\to Q'\) and \(\phi:T'\to T\). The transformed history is:

\[
\widetilde h=f\circ h\circ\phi.
\]

| Property | Sufficient conditions for two-way preservation |
| --- | --- |
| Constancy or nonconstancy | \(f\) injective on the relevant image and \(\phi\) surjective onto the history domain |
| Traversal order | Additional order structure and increasing bijective \(\phi\) |
| Continuity | Homeomorphisms of relevant spaces and domains |
| Equivalent derivative structure | Suitable diffeomorphisms of spaces and parameters |
| Zero derivative vector at corresponding points | Injective \(Df\), \(\phi'\ne0\), and differentiability |
| Equal curve length | For example, isometric \(f\) and increasing bijective interval reparametrization |

A homeomorphism is a continuous bijection with continuous inverse. A diffeomorphism is a smooth bijection with smooth inverse on the compared structures; weaker local conditions may suffice for one derivative.

These rows are not a chain of jointly necessary conditions. Isometry, for example, is sufficient but stronger than required for one particular curve.

**Constancy proof.** Composition preserves a constant \(h\). Conversely, constancy of \(f(h(\phi(u)))\) and injectivity of \(f\) imply constancy of \(h(\phi(u))\). Surjectivity of \(\phi\) reaches every \(h(t)\), so \(h\) is constant.

Surjectivity matters. Observing only a resting subinterval does not establish constancy of the entire history.

**Derivative proof.** In smooth coordinates:

\[
\frac{d\widetilde h}{d\lambda}
=Df_{h(\phi(\lambda))}
\left(\frac{dh}{dt}\bigg|_{t=\phi(\lambda)}\right)\phi'(\lambda).
\]

With \(\phi'\ne0\) and injective \(Df\), the right side vanishes exactly when \(dh/dt=0\) at the corresponding point. Numerical speeds need not agree; norms and units may change too.

**Length proof.** An isometry preserves every partition-sum distance. Increasing bijective interval reparametrization pairs partitions between domains. Their suprema are therefore equal.

**Counterexamples connecting Time and Reference.** Take \(h(t)=t\).

- The coordinate map \(f(x)=x^3\) is a bijection and homeomorphism of the line, but its inverse is not differentiable at zero. The history \(f(h(t))=t^3\) has zero derivative at zero, while \(h'(0)=1\).
- The reparametrization \(t=\lambda^3\) is also an increasing bijection, but \(\phi'(0)=0\). The transformed history \(\lambda^3\) has zero rate at zero without interval constancy.

Both preserve nonconstancy and continuity. Both fail to preserve zero-rate criteria because regularity conditions fail. Cubic coordinates are not a compatible smooth chart at zero for the line's standard differential structure.

**Physical limit.** Formal reparametrization does not prove a physical clock can realize those readings with every requested property. That needs a clock model. Differential and physical-time concepts use [F-S06](../Foundation/Research/Sources.md#s06), and topology uses [F-S07](../Foundation/Research/Sources.md#s07).

## P03

**Constancy on a partial order differs from comparing every pair.**

**Premises.** Let \(T\) have partial order \(\preceq\), \(Q\) ordinary equality, and \(h:T\to Q\). Assume \(h(t)=h(u)\) whenever \(t\) and \(u\) are comparable.

Define \(t\approx u\) when a finite sequence \(t=t_0,\ldots,t_n=u\) connects them with each neighbouring pair comparable in either direction.

**Conclusion.** \(h\) is constant on each \(\approx\)-class. With only one class, \(h\) is constant on all \(T\).

**Proof.** Each step gives equality; transitivity yields \(h(t_0)=h(t_n)\). The relation is reflexive, symmetric by sequence reversal, and transitive by concatenation, so \(\approx\) forms equivalence classes.

**Limit.** Two components lacking such a connecting sequence can have different values without violating the premise.

The smallest example is incomparable \(a,b\) with \(h(a)=0,h(b)=1\). The function is nonconstant without an ordered change from \(a\) to \(b\). Conversely, a branching order \(a\preceq b\), \(a\preceq c\) forces all three values equal through \(a\), even if \(b,c\) are incomparable.

**Scientific meaning.** For partial domains, interpreting “two different values exist” as temporal change requires a comparison context. Different field values at spacelike events do not automatically describe one moving object.

This mathematical result does not establish that causality is always a partial order, every event lies on one object's history, or material identity emerges from order. Causal and proper-time limits remain those of [Time](../Foundation/Core/Time.md).

## What can be simplified

Coordinates, parameters, and state groupings can all be maps, but preserve different properties. Explanation does not require six separate substances; it requires distinguishing each structure's mathematical and physical tasks.

P01 establishes comparison consistency, P02 property-preservation conditions, and P03 temporal limits for nontotal orders. None derives physical geometry or dynamics from functions alone.

# Evidence

## Conclusions are relative to a possibility class

Knowledge of motion requires more than data \(y\): an admissible history class \(\mathcal H\), comparison reference, and observation map \(\mathcal O:\mathcal H\to Y\) specify what remains possible after observing.

Define:

\[
\mathcal H_y=\{h\in\mathcal H:\mathcal O(h)=y\}.
\]

Here \(y\) always belongs to \(\mathcal O(\mathcal H)\), so its compatible class is nonempty. An empty class signals model–data incompatibility, not evidence for every conclusion simultaneously.

[Evidence Foundation](../Foundation/Core/Evidence.md) supplies the basis; [P04](Reduction.md#p04) develops the functional criterion.

## P06

**Identifiability is property factorization through data.**

**Premises.** Let \(P:\mathcal H\to W\) be a property; for yes–no questions, \(W=\{0,1\}\). Reference and equivalence conventions are fixed.

**Conclusion.** A unique \(\widehat P:\mathcal O(\mathcal H)\to W\) determining \(P(h)\) from data for every history exists if and only if:

\[
\mathcal O(h_1)=\mathcal O(h_2)
\ \Longrightarrow\
P(h_1)=P(h_2).
\]

**Proof.** Apply P04 with \(X=\mathcal H\), \(C=\mathcal O\) restricted to its image, and \(A=P\).

For one particular datum, constancy of \(P\) on \(\mathcal H_y\) suffices; global model uniqueness is unnecessary.

### Knowing motion without reconstructing the history

Take continuous line histories, a fixed reference, and exact data \(q(0)=0,q(1)=1\). Every compatible history is nonconstant, so position change on the interval is known.

Yet \(q_1(t)=t\) and \(q_2(t)=t^2\) give equal endpoint data and different histories. Information insufficient for full reconstruction can suffice for one motion conclusion.

Conversely, \(q(0)=q(1)=0\) admits both rest and \(q(t)=t(1-t)\). The same property is not identifiable on this class.

### Two conditions that must remain distinct

If \(\sim_{\mathrm{phys}}\) denotes physical redundancy, \(P\) must first be constant on its classes to be physically well-defined. Only then is constancy of \(P\) on observation fibres tested.

Physical classes and observation fibres may have different sizes. Limited observation can merge physically distinct states. Data differences also require calibration and representational checks before being called physical differences.

**Limit.** This establishes uniqueness in an ideal deterministic model, not stability under disturbances or physically exact measurement procedures.

## P07

**Data reduction cannot increase structural identifiability.**

**Premises.** Observations are related by:

\[
\mathcal O_2=K\circ\mathcal O_1.
\]

The second data result solely from deterministic processing of the same first data, with no additional input.

**Conclusion.** A property determinable from \(\mathcal O_2\) is determinable from \(\mathcal O_1\). The converse can fail.

**Proof.** If \(\mathcal O_1(h_1)=\mathcal O_1(h_2)\), applying \(K\) produces equal \(\mathcal O_2\) outputs. Classes merged by \(\mathcal O_1\) are therefore no larger than those merged by \(\mathcal O_2\). Constancy on larger classes implies constancy on smaller ones.

Directly, if \(P=\widehat P_2\circ\mathcal O_2\), then:

\[
P=(\widehat P_2\circ K)\circ\mathcal O_1.
\]

**Loss example.** On all line histories, let \(P(h)=1\) when \(q(0)\ne q(1)\), otherwise zero. It is always determined by \(\mathcal O_1(h)=(q(0),q(1))\). If \(K\) retains only the initial position, \(q(t)=t\) and rest at zero have identical outputs but different \(P\). The converse fails.

For data \((0,1)\), this property also proves motion. But \(P=0\) does not prove rest: a history can return to its starting point. “Different endpoints” is not equivalent to “ever moved”.

**Consequence.** Reprocessing data that merge two histories cannot force their separation. Additional models or assumptions can narrow \(\mathcal H\), but change the premises. Adding a sensor or experimental condition is not merely applying \(K\) to old data.

This concerns deterministic maps, not all Shannon information theorems, statistical optimality, or algorithmic performance. Processing may improve noisy-data estimation or presentation; this theorem does not assess estimator performance.

## P08

**A length lower bound from positions with bounded errors.**

**Additional premises.** Let \(q:[a,b]\to Q\) be continuous in one positive metric space \((Q,d)\), with consistent reference and units. At exact times \(a=t_0<\cdots<t_n=b\), positions \(y_i\in Q\) satisfy deterministic bounds:

\[
d(y_i,q(t_i))\le\varepsilon_i,\qquad \varepsilon_i\ge0.
\]

These bounds need independent justification. They are not automatically certainty intervals derived from metrological standard deviations.

**Conclusion.** For curve length defined by partition supremum:

\[
L(q)\ge
\sum_{i=1}^{n}
\max\{0,\ d(y_i,y_{i-1})-\varepsilon_i-\varepsilon_{i-1}\}.
\tag{4}
\]

**Proof.** The triangle inequality gives:

\[
d(y_i,y_{i-1})
\le \varepsilon_i+d(q(t_i),q(t_{i-1}))+\varepsilon_{i-1}.
\]

Nonnegativity bounds each true distance below by the maximum in (4). The partition's true-distance sum is bounded above by the supremum \(L(q)\).

**Meaning.** A positive right side makes every premise-satisfying curve nonconstant, despite nonunique full reconstruction. This connects geometry, uncertainty, and property identifiability concretely.

If \(L(q)\) is finite and \(b-a>0\) is the relevant duration, length-based average speed is bounded below by (4) divided by \(b-a\). This differs from displacement divided by time.

**Example.** One-dimensional data \(y_0=0,y_1=3,y_2=0\), each with error at most \(1/4\), imply \(L(q)\ge5\), despite equal endpoint data. Exact positions give a bound of 6. Values use consistent units or normalized quantities.

**Limits.** A zero right side does not prove rest. The bound need not be sharp and determines neither cause, full direction, nor velocity profile. Lorentzian “distance” is not substituted for a positive metric. Moving-reference observations first require consistent transformation under P01.

## P09

**Rate bounds constrain hidden motion without necessarily excluding it.**

**Additional premises.** The history satisfies a Lipschitz bound:

\[
d(q(t),q(u))\le V|t-u|,\qquad V\ge0.
\]

This assumes regularity and bounded change in the selected metric; continuity alone does not imply it.

If \(q(a)=q(b)=x_0\), then:

\[
d(q(t),x_0)
\le V\min\{t-a,b-t\}
\le\frac{V(b-a)}2.
\tag{5}
\]

**Proof.** Apply the Lipschitz bound to endpoint \(a\) and endpoint \(b\) and take the smaller bound.

On the line, \(q(t)=x_0+V\min\{t-a,b-t\}\) reaches height \(V(b-a)/2\). It is Lipschitz and nonconstant for \(V>0\). Equal endpoints and a positive rate bound therefore do not prove rest.

A smooth uniform-sampling example is:

\[
q(t)=A\sin(2\pi t/\Delta),\qquad
0<|A|\le \frac{V\Delta}{2\pi}.
\]

All positions at \(t=n\Delta\) vanish, but the history changes with \(|q'(t)|\le V\). This connects Foundation's sampling ambiguity to an additional rate bound.

**Further consequence.** Exact data with \(d(q(a),q(b))>V(b-a)\) contradict the bounded-rate model. A premise must be reassessed; selecting a history violating all premises is invalid.

For \(V=0\), the Lipschitz bound itself forces constancy. Constancy then follows from an interval-wide assumption, not two records alone.

## Uniqueness is not stability

P06 asks whether ideal data determine one answer. Another question is whether small data changes produce only small conclusion changes.

An injective map can have a highly sensitive inverse. Conversely, a noninjective reduction can reliably retain a binary property when all compatible histories agree on it.

P08 uses explicit error bounds for one stronger justification. It does not resolve every disturbance, identity ambiguity, projection, or model error. These epistemic distinctions preserve the care established in [Evidence Foundation](../Foundation/Core/Evidence.md).

# Limits

## Scientific relations have different strengths

Connecting concepts is not deriving conclusions. A relation's role determines its justification:

| Relation type | Justification | What does not follow alone |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Definitional | Consistent use of one definition | Physical causation |
| Mathematical implication | All theorem premises hold in one structure | Physical existence of that structure |
| Representational dependency | A construction needs specified structure | That structure's ontological priority |
| Empirical constraint | Data, observation models, experimental domain | Unrestricted universality |
| Conceptual interpretation | Arguments clarifying distinctions | A theorem or new empirical discovery |
| Formal analogy | Explicitly shared patterns and maps | Identical meaning of all mapped objects |

Foundation's relation map includes several types. Synthesis does not promote every connection to logical implication.

## Conditions for composing arguments

If \(\Gamma\Rightarrow A\) and \(\Delta,A\Rightarrow B\), then \(B\) follows under \(\Gamma\cup\Delta\), provided symbols have compatible meanings and premises are jointly satisfiable.

This is ordinary logic. The scientific issue is contextual compatibility, not arrow shape alone.

**Valid composition.** Positions use a known fixed reference, errors are genuinely bounded in the same positive metric, and P08's right side is positive. Every premise-satisfying history then has positive length and is nonconstant.

**Invalid composition.** A fixed centre position and the zero-derivative constancy theorem do not establish rest of an entire body. The theorem establishes only constancy of the represented centre coordinates, not an unrepresented orientation.

**Framework incompatibility.** Newtonian and relativistic simultaneity cannot alternate as one identical global relation. Approximation requires regime boundaries and mapping rules; sharing the word “time” supplies neither.

## Four noninterchangeable questions

1. **Does the model admit possibilities?** Compatibility inference requires nonempty \(\mathcal H_y\).
2. **Is the property well-defined?** Predicates must respect the chosen physical equivalence.
3. **Do data distinguish it sufficiently?** Predicates must be constant on compatible observational classes.
4. **Is the result stable and empirically supported?** This requires disturbances, observation models, and usage domains to be assessed.

A covariant equation does not answer all four. A well-defined theoretical predicate can remain unidentifiable from available data. Ideal uniqueness does not guarantee inverse stability.

## Conclusions needing additional premises

| Desired conclusion | Available foundation | Required addition |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Nonconstant history | States, domain, equality | Meaningful comparison across changing contexts or references |
| Change is spatial motion | State history | Position, orientation, or spatial-arrangement interpretation |
| Physical speed value | Local change structure | Metric or norm, clock parameter, units, regularity |
| Closed reduced evolution | Reduction map | Full evolution and fibre preservation |
| Fixed density implies zero current | Density information | Conservation and sufficient domain or boundary conditions |
| Zero total current implies every part rests | Aggregate current | State relations excluding component cancellation |
| Samples establish interval rest | Discrete records | History restrictions genuinely excluding hidden change |
| Measurements determine state | Selected observables | Separation or injectivity on relevant states |
| Stationary probability law implies fixed realization | Process distribution | Much stronger restrictions; stationarity alone is insufficient |
| Motion experience determines a unique source | Perceptual reports | Psychophysical model, controlled conditions, sufficient source information |

This does not recommend adopting every addition. It marks where derivation stops without a premise.

## Sharpening zero-derivative conditions

Foundation distinguishes:

- Zero derivative everywhere on an interval, with suitable differentiability, gives constancy by the mean value theorem.
- Zero derivative almost everywhere requires additional conditions.

A real function \(q\) is absolutely continuous on \([a,b]\), \(a<b\), when for every \(\varepsilon>0\) some \(\delta>0\) ensures that every finite family of subintervals with disjoint interiors and total length below \(\delta\) has total absolute change \(\sum_i|q(b_i)-q(a_i)|<\varepsilon\).

For such functions:

\[
q(t)=q(a)+\int_a^t q'(u)\,du.
\]

If \(q'=0\) almost everywhere, the integral vanishes and \(q\) is constant. Absolute continuity restores an inference invalid for arbitrary continuous functions. The Cantor function is a standard nonconstant continuous example with derivative zero almost everywhere. [N02](Sources.md#n02)

This develops the foundations without declaring every continuous function a physical motion. For finite-dimensional vector curves, the argument applies componentwise.

## Errors caused by omitting premises

P05 assumes deterministic full evolution; it does not prove universal determinism of motion.

P08 assumes deterministic error bounds; it does not turn every statistical uncertainty interval into a guaranteed length bound.

P11 assumes conservative continuity. With a source \(\sigma\), the equation becomes \(\partial_t\rho+\nabla\cdot J=\sigma\). Stationary density then implies \(\nabla\cdot J=\sigma\), not necessarily zero.

P12 assumes uniform phase to obtain shift-invariant distributions. Without it, stationarity need not hold.

## Why one formal criterion is not one ontology

P04 applies to many non-motion objects. It explains descriptive sufficiency for a conclusion, but selects neither physical space, time, existence, nor causes of change.

Mass density and probability density remain different despite similarly shaped conservation equations. Mathematical partial orders are not automatically causal. Shared forms supply reasoning tools, not permission to transfer entire interpretations.

The six foundations are not derived as six independent ontological constituents. Nor are they all physically reduced to equivalence. Distinction criteria still need framework-specific meaning.

## Questions remaining open

Time's nature, deepest-scale spacetime continuity, and individual trajectories in quantum interpretations are not settled by map theorems.

Perception also does not reduce to one observation rule. Inherited experiments constrain interpretations under particular conditions. Calling instrument outputs and experience reports “data” does not remove their separate mechanistic questions.

Architectural minimality remains open. P04 can consolidate particular reasoning redundancies while physical meanings and premise justifications remain diverse.

Retained relations have arguments with explicit domains. This boundary permits further development without passing hidden premises into new conclusions.

# Overview

## From distinctions to conclusions about motion

A motion description connects distinguished states, temporal contexts, spatial arrangements, and comparison rules. Knowledge of motion adds evidence relations. Connecting these structures sharpens the question beyond whether “something changes”.

The starting question is: **which distinctions are retained, relative to which comparison, and which conclusions remain justified by the available information?**

This is conceptual synthesis, not a single ontological definition. Classical particle models can compare positions or configurations. Quantum state rays, position densities, and currents are different objects. Perceptual motion experience is not definitionally identical to one external object's history.

[State](../Foundation/Core/State.md), [Space](../Foundation/Core/Space.md), and [Evidence](../Foundation/Core/Evidence.md) establish these distinctions. This synthesis develops their consequences through examinable arguments.

## Three mutually constraining conditions

| Condition | Scientific question | Consequence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Consistent comparison | Are reference and state correctly transformed together? | Relabelling must not change statements intended to remain equivalent |
| Descriptive sufficiency | Are discarded distinctions still needed for conclusions or evolution? | Simpler descriptions need not support the same laws or predicates |
| Evidential sufficiency | Do all data-compatible possibilities agree on the conclusion? | A property can be known without reconstructing the entire history |

These differ. A coordinate-consistent model may remain unidentifiable from data. Observations can distinguish many states while using an uncalibrated reference. A reduction may retain position exactly while discarding momentum needed for prediction.

Invariance, prediction, and empirical justification therefore cannot substitute for one another.

## Shared mathematical structure

Let \(C:X\to Z=C(X)\) merge some possibilities in \(X\). A quantity or conclusion \(A:X\to W\) is expressible through \(Z\) alone exactly when:

\[
C(x_1)=C(x_2)\ \Longrightarrow\ A(x_1)=A(x_2).
\]

Then there is a unique \(\bar A:Z\to W\) such that:

\[
A=\bar A\circ C.
\]

[P04](Reduction.md#p04) supplies the proof. This is an elementary result about functions and equivalence classes, not a new Motion axiom.

Its synthesizing power comes from **different uses with different premises**:

- If \(C\) removes physical redundancy, the condition tests whether a predicate is well-defined on the intended physical states.
- If \(C\) reduces information, it tests descriptive sufficiency for a quantity or operation.
- If \(C\) observes histories, it tests conclusion identifiability.

These meanings of “merged” must not be equated. Physical equivalence needs theoretical justification; one observation's indistinguishability does not establish it.

## Results from connecting foundations

[P01](Comparison.md#p01) shows why comparison rules must change with state representations, explaining how relative motion survives time-dependent coordinate changes.

[P02](Comparison.md#p02) separates preserving nonconstancy from preserving rates. A bijection sufficient for state distinctions need not suffice for calculus. [P03](Comparison.md#p03) adds limits for partially ordered temporal domains.

[P05](Reduction.md#p05) applies the same criterion to transformations and evolution: a reduced operation is well-defined only if merged states do not produce different reduced outputs. Position alone can fail as a predictive state even under deterministic full evolution.

[P06](Evidence.md#p06) and [P07](Evidence.md#p07) explain why knowing motion occurs need not require knowing all its details, and why deterministic processing of identical data cannot resolve structural ambiguity.

[P08](Evidence.md#p08) combines geometry, time, and error bounds into a lower bound on motion length. [P09](Evidence.md#p09) uses a maximum-rate bound to constrain hidden motion without automatically proving rest.

[P10](Stationarity.md#p10) through [P13](Stationarity.md#p13) distinguish constant observables, distributions, statistics, currents, and changing representations. “Rest” loses a unique meaning when the allegedly constant object is unspecified.

## Additional structure remains necessary

Shared reasoning forms do not produce forces, motion laws, physical geometry, universal clocks, or perceptual mechanisms. Those require premises beyond the existence of a map.

Reduced-evolution criteria matter only after full evolution is supplied. Conservation equations constrain currents only after the equation and boundary conditions are assumed. Measurement-based length bounds require a positive metric, a shared reference, and valid error bounds.

Knowledge develops through an explicit chain: foundations supply structure, added premises select context, and arguments derive consequences. Omitting premises from the statement does not make a consequence more fundamental.

## Limits of unification

Factorization unifies **tests of sufficiency** without reducing all meanings of motion to one mathematical object. It does not derive space–time identity, universally individual identity, or universally smooth trajectories.

The defensible synthesis is mutually explanatory conditional relations. Physical object meanings, admissible histories, temporal structures, and evidence types remain distinct. [Limits](Limits.md) examines these boundaries; [Trace.tsv](Trace.tsv) links each result to its origins and conditions.

# Reduction

## The same equation, three meanings

State equivalence, coarse-graining, and observational indistinguishability can all be maps merging alternatives. Their reasons differ:

| Merger | What is treated as equal | Required justification |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Representational redundancy | Physical states according to a theory | Theoretical structure and interpretation |
| Descriptive reduction | Deliberately retained information | Sufficiency for a particular question |
| Observational indistinguishability | Possible generated data | Observation model and possibility class |

[State](../Foundation/Core/State.md) distinguishes the first two; [Evidence](../Foundation/Core/Evidence.md) supplies the third. Their relation allows a shared mathematical criterion without equating physical meanings.

## P04

**Factorization through a reduced description.**

**Premises.** Let \(X,W\) be sets, \(C:X\to Z\) surjective, and \(A:X\to W\) a function. Each \(z\) represents the possibilities in its fibre \(C^{-1}(\{z\})\).

**Conclusion.** A unique \(\bar A:Z\to W\) with \(A=\bar A\circ C\) exists if and only if:

\[
C(x_1)=C(x_2)\ \Longrightarrow\ A(x_1)=A(x_2).
\tag{1}
\]

**Necessity.** If \(\bar A\) exists, equal inputs \(C(x_1)=C(x_2)\) have equal outputs, giving \(A(x_1)=A(x_2)\).

**Sufficiency.** For each \(z\in Z\), take the value \(A(x)\) on the fibre \(C^{-1}(\{z\})\). Surjectivity makes the fibre nonempty; condition (1) makes this value independent of representative, defining \(\bar A(z)\).

**Uniqueness.** Every \(z=C(x)\) must satisfy \(\bar A(z)=A(x)\); no alternative output is possible.

This elementary theorem about functions on equivalence classes is not a new physical law. [N01](Sources.md#n01) discusses the topological form with continuity conditions. The proof here starts at set level.

**What does not follow.** Existence of \(\bar A\) as a function guarantees neither continuity, measurability, smoothness, computability, nor physical measurability. If \(C\) is a topological quotient map and \(A\) continuous, the quotient's universal property makes \(\bar A\) continuous. Extra properties are not free without their conditions.

## Motion as a well-defined predicate

Let \(\pi:\mathcal H\to\mathcal H/{\sim}\) merge history representations expressing the same physical state according to the theory, including the reference. A predicate \(M:\mathcal H\to\{0,1\}\) is meaningful on physical classes only if:

\[
h_1\sim h_2\ \Longrightarrow\ M(h_1)=M(h_2).
\]

This applies P04 with \(C=\pi\). A predicate changing under representational redundancy is not well-defined at its claimed physical level.

P01 illustrates how transforming comparison rules together with states preserves such conclusions. Declaring every transformation “redundancy”, however, adds ontology not justified by P04.

## P05

**When operations descend to reduced descriptions.**

**Premises.** Let \(C:X\to Z\) be surjective and \(T:X\to X\) an operation.

**Conclusion.** A unique operation \(\bar T:Z\to Z\) satisfying:

\[
\bar T\circ C=C\circ T
\tag{2}
\]

exists exactly when:

\[
C(x_1)=C(x_2)
\ \Longrightarrow\
C(T(x_1))=C(T(x_2)).
\tag{3}
\]

**Proof.** Apply P04 to \(A=C\circ T\). Condition (3) is precisely condition (1).

This establishes sufficiency for a specified operation, not preservation of every state distinction or operation.

### Reference transformations may fail to descend

Take \(X=\mathbb R^2\), \(C(x,y)=x\), and rotation:

\[
T(x,y)=(-y,x).
\]

States \((0,0)\) and \((0,1)\) both reduce to zero. After rotation their reduced values are zero and \(-1\). Condition (3) fails.

Thus no single rule transforms old \(x\) into new \(x\) for all points under this rotation after discarding \(y\). Reduction has lost information needed for transformation.

**Cross-foundation consequence.** Descriptions equivalent for one reference need not suffice for changing references. The rotation is valid; the one-component description is insufficient.

### Reduced evolution requires closure

Suppose an autonomous deterministic evolution \(\Phi_t:X\to X\), \(t\ge0\), is supplied with:

\[
\Phi_0=\mathrm{id},\qquad
\Phi_{t+s}=\Phi_t\circ\Phi_s.
\]

This is an **additional dynamical-model premise**, not a kinematic consequence.

If condition (3) holds for every \(\Phi_t\), P05 yields \(\Psi_t:Z\to Z\) with:

\[
\Psi_t\circ C=C\circ\Phi_t.
\]

**Further derivation.**

\[
\Psi_{t+s}(C(x))
=C(\Phi_{t+s}(x))
=\Psi_t(\Psi_s(C(x))).
\]

Surjectivity of \(C\) gives \(\Psi_{t+s}=\Psi_t\circ\Psi_s\), and similarly \(\Psi_0=\mathrm{id}\). The semigroup property therefore descends at set level. Regularity and other physical properties require separate conditions.

**Failure example.** For a classical free particle with \(m>0\):

\[
\Phi_t(q,p)=\left(q+\frac{p}{m}t,p\right),\qquad C(q,p)=q.
\]

Initial states \((0,0)\) and \((0,m)\) have equal positions. At \(t>0\), positions are zero and \(t\). Position evolution is therefore not closed as a function of current position on this state class.

This assumes the free-particle law. It clarifies configuration versus phase state in [F-S22](../Foundation/Research/Sources.md#s22), without deriving that law from P05.

**Valid restriction.** Fixing momentum to one known value in advance can make position sufficient on the narrower class. Sufficiency changes because the class is restricted, not because position supplies momentum information.

## Merging need not preserve continuity

Quotients can change topology. Algebraically identical diagrams do not guarantee a manifold or the same rates on the reduced space.

Sharing a fibre also does not guarantee a physical path inside it. For example, let \(X=\{0,1\}\) be discrete, \(C\) constant, and allow only continuous histories from a connected interval. No nonconstant history is allowed despite noninjective \(C\).

This sharpens “reduction can hide change”: lost distinctions permit structural ambiguity, but actual history ambiguity still depends on the admissible class \(\mathcal H\).

## What can and cannot be unified

P04 supplies one reasoning pattern for retained-information sufficiency. P05 applies it to both transformations and dynamics.

Physical reasons for merging, relevant operations, and history-restricting laws remain distinct. A reduction may answer one question adequately while failing another.

[Evidence](Evidence.md) applies the criterion to observations. [Stationarity](Stationarity.md) examines descriptive constancy versus state constancy.

# Review

Review date: **2 November 2026**.

## What was examined

Review included all six foundations and their structure, sources, relations, claims, glossary, questions, and initial assessment. At the synthesis stage, all 16 source files matched the pre-reorganization snapshot hashes. This repository edition subsequently translates the prose into English; Origins records both identities.

Arguments were evaluated for whether conclusions follow stated premises, terms retain their meanings, and counterexamples defeat excessive generalizations.

P01–P13 are not 13 new postulates. Several apply the same elementary result in different contexts; separate identifiers trace differing premises and meanings.

## Separation of results from sources

At the original synthesis stage, Foundation was moved into one subfolder without content changes. [Origins.tsv](Origins.tsv) now records the original snapshot and English-edition identities and their locations.

New results remain in Synthesis. Sources records additional references; Trace records premises. The refinements below remain separate from the foundation; translating the edition does not silently add them to its scientific claims.

## Refinements of the original source reading

| Finding | Original source | Synthesis refinement | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Noninjectivity does not guarantee an admissible moving history within a fibre | State, “Equivalence and retained information” | Reduction adds history classes and a connected-domain/discrete-state example | Scope refinement, not rejection of “can hide” |
| Instantaneous global-phase equivalence does not fix the evolution equation after time-dependent phase changes | State and Change, quantum pure states | P13 derives an additional generator term | Added consequence under Schrödinger premises |
| Constant samples are insufficient, but different endpoints can establish a property | Evidence, identifiability and sampling | P06 separates property detection from reconstruction; P08 adds errors | Deeper reasoning |
| Partial orders need clarification of “changing” | Time, order structure | P03 restricts conclusions to comparable pairs and comparison classes | Conceptual qualification |
| “Stationary” can refer to several objects | Change and Glossary | P10–P12 separate observables, densities, currents, statistical laws, realizations | Meaning separation |

This review did not justify silently changing the foundations. Refinements remain independently examinable results.

## Counterexamples and retained conditions

| Test | Error prevented | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| \(q=t,\ x'=x-t\), with transformed comparison rule | Zero coordinates erase original relative motion | P01 preserves the comparison history |
| \(x'=x^3\), \(t=\lambda^3\) | Bijections suffice to preserve zero derivatives | P02 requires regularity |
| Incomparable contexts | Different values automatically imply one object's temporal change | P03 limits inference |
| \(C(x,y)=x,\ T(x,y)=(-y,x)\) | Transformations always remain possible after discarding information | P05 fails precisely when fibres are not preserved |
| Equal-position free particles with different momenta | Full determinism predicts position from position alone | Reduced evolution is not closed on that class |
| Endpoint data \((0,1)\) versus \((0,0)\) | Motion detection equals reconstruction or merely endpoint difference | P06–P07 distinguish properties and quantification |
| Noisy data with deterministic error bounds | Standard deviation guarantees motion absolutely | P08 states actual bound premises |
| Tent curves and intersample sinusoids | Positive rate bounds eliminate all hidden motion | P09 bounds amplitude without proving rest |
| Circulating and opposing-component currents | Zero divergence or total current means every part rests | P11 retains the distinctions |
| Uniform-phase oscillation | Stationary statistics imply fixed individual paths | P12 proves fixed joint laws with nonconstant histories |
| Time-dependent quantum phase | Original equation holds without generator transformation | P13 gives the consistent extra-term sign |

## Proofs and additional checks

General proofs appear in result documents; they are not inferred from counts of passing examples. Additional checks targeted algebra and example conditions:

| Check | Finite scope examined |
| --- | --- |
| P04 factorization | 162 map pairs on a three-element domain, including unique factor functions |
| P05 operation descent | 162 operations and reductions on a three-element domain |
| P07 data simplification | 1,728 map–predicate combinations |
| P03 partial-order constancy | 19 labelled three-element partial orders; 152 value assignments |
| P08 inequality | 1,000 one-dimensional polygonal cases using exact rationals |
| P09 excursion bound | 21 positions on a peak-bound-attaining example |
| P12 phase shifts | 44 discrete uniform-phase permutations as illustrations |
| P13 phase generator | Five complex evaluations of the \(-\hbar\dot\theta\) sign |

These finite checks agreed with the statements. They do not prove all domains, continuous probabilities from discrete samples, or physical applicability.

During review P07's example was clarified to separate “different endpoints” from “ever moved”: returning histories have equal endpoints but remain nonconstant.

## Claim-type assessment

P01–P10 mainly concern functions, orders, differentiation, and metrics under stated premises. P11 needs conservation; P12 assumes a probabilistic example; P13 needs quantum evolution.

No new empirical results are claimed. Perception findings and quantum or relativistic limits retain their inherited source domains. Shared mass/probability conservation forms do not establish identical quantities.

## Artifact checks and evaluation limits

Local links, result anchors, source references, trace tables, and formula delimiters were checked. Foundation/Checksums.tsv is regenerated for this English edition. Project checksums assess byte equality, not scientific truth.

Review is internal, without independent peer review, proof assistants, or systematic coverage of all literature. Failure to unify the foundations into one ontology does not prove permanent impossibility.

The retained result is a conditional reasoning structure stronger than the initial relation list: shared sufficiency criteria, geometric consequences of evidence, and traceable limits on stationarity and reduction. Universal minimality and new laws of all Motion are not claimed.

# Sources

## Role of sources

The primary synthesis source is the complete Foundation: six core files, architecture, glossary, 45 relations, 43 claims, references, and initial review. Organization and relation counts are not automatic proof.

P01–P13 present arguments from stated premises. Elementary function, invariance, and inequality results are not claimed as new literature discoveries. “Synthesis result” means a result obtained in this connected exposition.

No fresh survey of all motion theories is attempted. Additional references address only three gaps: quotient structure, absolute continuity, and mass conservation as a comparison.

## Connections to Foundation

| Internal source | Portions used | Synthesis role |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [State](../Foundation/Core/State.md) | Equivalence, reduction, observables, identity | Retained distinctions and reasons for merging |
| [Time](../Foundation/Core/Time.md) | Order, parameters, duration, relativistic limits | What survives temporal or parameter reinterpretation |
| [Space](../Foundation/Core/Space.md) | Configurations, metrics, fields, material currents | Spatial interpretation and geometric limits |
| [Reference](../Foundation/Core/Reference.md) | Comparison maps and transformations | P01–P02 and reduced-operation checks |
| [Change](../Foundation/Core/Change.md) | Histories, regularity, length, circle example | Geometric bounds and constancy distinctions |
| [Evidence](../Foundation/Core/Evidence.md) | Compatible classes, sampling, projection, perception | Property factorization and inference limits |
| [Architecture](../Foundation/Structure/Architecture.md) and [Boundaries](../Foundation/Structure/Boundaries.md) | Node status and foundational–derived limits | Prevents reading architecture as natural axioms |
| [Relations.tsv](../Foundation/Structure/Relations.tsv) and [Claims.tsv](../Foundation/Research/Claims.tsv) | Conditions and claim types | Reassessment points, not independent logical authority |
| [Questions](../Foundation/Research/Questions.md) and [Review](../Foundation/Research/Review.md) | Open issues and counterexamples | Limits claim expansion |

## Inherited references

**F-Sxx** refers to **Sxx** in [Foundation Sources](../Foundation/Research/Sources.md). The prefix distinguishes namespaces without changing source identities.

| Label | Main relevance |
| --- | --- |
| F-S01 | Equivalence relations and partial orders |
| F-S05, F-S06 | References, temporal structure, geometric regularity |
| F-S07 | Topology, continuity, connectedness |
| F-S09 | Global-phase equivalence and quantum stationary states |
| F-S10, F-S11 | Probability currents and particles on a circle |
| F-S12 | Limits of identical-particle label interpretations |
| F-S13, F-S14, F-S21 | Stimulus and perception inference limits |
| F-S15 | Conditional reconstruction in bandlimited signal classes |
| F-S18 | Measurement uncertainty versus known or bounded errors |
| F-S19, F-S20 | Relational-time models and discrete-spacetime proposals |
| F-S22 | Configurations, phase states, classical prediction |

This table establishes relevance, not attribution of every result to those references. Proofs and added premises remain in synthesis documents.

## Additional references

### N01

Romyar Sharifi. **Point-Set Topology**, Chapter 2, §2.3; especially Theorem 2.3.11.

[Author's material, UCLA](https://www.math.ucla.edu/~sharifi/notes/topology-ch02.html).

Type: author's scientific notes. Examined portion: functions constant on quotient fibres and continuity of descended functions. A standard reference for P04's topological form; the set-level proof appears directly in Reduction.

### N02

John K. Hunter. **Notes on Partial Differential Equations**, revised 18 June 2014. University of California, Davis. Appendix 3.A, especially Theorem 3.60 and singular functions.

[Author's notes](https://www.math.ucdavis.edu/~hunter/pdes/pde_notes.pdf).

Type: author's scientific notes. Examined portion: absolute continuity and the fundamental theorem of calculus; the Cantor function limits generalizations. Does not expand the core into partial differential equations.

### N03

Richard Fitzpatrick. **Mass Conservation**, fluid-mechanics teaching material. University of Texas at Austin.

[Author's material](https://farside.ph.utexas.edu/teaching/336L/Fluidhtml/node10.html).

Type: author's scientific material. Examined portion: density, velocity, and mass continuity. Explains why P11's conservation form is a model premise with quantity-specific meaning.

## Reading and proof limits

The indicated additional-source portions were checked on **2 November 2026**, not surveyed as entire manuscripts.

Empirical facts remain those researched in Foundation. Synthesis produces no new experimental data and establishes no universal perceptual mechanism.

P12 uses strict stationarity and a random-phase example with a full distribution-shift proof. It infers no further property such as ergodicity.

Numerical examples use normalized quantities or consistent units. Mass, length, and physical parameters receive positivity conditions and meanings at their points of use.

[Trace.tsv](Trace.tsv) links premises, results, foundations, and references. main_dependencies lists only results used in primary proofs; connections lists associations or applications, not automatically proof premises. P13, for example, connects to P01–P02 but derives directly from Schrödinger evolution and the product rule.

[Origins.tsv](Origins.tsv) records original-source and English-edition byte identities.

# Stationarity

## What is claimed to remain constant?

“Stationary” may concern a state, selected quantity, distribution, process statistics, or representation. Motion conclusions require specifying both object and equality type.

Connections among [State](../Foundation/Core/State.md), [Change](../Foundation/Core/Change.md), and [Evidence](../Foundation/Core/Evidence.md) separate several implications precisely.

## P10

**Constant observations imply a constant state only when sufficiently distinguishing.**

**Premises.** Let \(h:T\to S\) and time-independent \(A:S\to Z\). If \(A\) is injective on \(h(T)\), then:

\[
A(h(t))\text{ constant}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
h(t)\text{ constant}.
\]

**Proof.** For all \(t,u\), equality \(A(h(t))=A(h(u))\) and image injectivity imply \(h(t)=h(u)\).

Conversely, a constant state always makes \(A\circ h\) constant. For a family \(A_i\), separating relevant states suffices; one scalar quantity is unnecessary.

**Theoretical limit.** State and injectivity are assessed after representational redundancy is fixed. Quantum state-to-outcome-distribution maps do not give classical definite values to all observables.

**Relation to P06.** P10 examines a state path through selected quantities. P06 examines a property across all data-compatible histories. Both use equal outputs, but differ in objects and quantifier scope.

If \(A\) depends on time, constant states can yield changing outputs: \(h(t)=0\), \(A_t(x)=x+t\). Conversely, \(h(t)=t\), \(A_t(x)=x-t\) yields constant output. Observation changes must separate system changes from changes in comparison or procedure.

## P11

**Stationary density constrains current divergence, not necessarily current.**

**Additional model premises.** In a specified domain and reference, sufficiently regular density \(\rho\) and current \(J\) obey source-free conservation:

\[
\partial_t\rho+\nabla\cdot J=0.
\tag{6}
\]

Such equations have different meanings in mass and probability conservation. [N03](Sources.md#n03) discusses mass conservation; [F-S10](../Foundation/Research/Sources.md#s10) supplies the quantum form.

**Conclusion.** If \(\partial_t\rho=0\), then \(\nabla\cdot J=0\). This does not imply \(J=0\).

**Proof and counterexample.** Substitution gives zero divergence. On a one-dimensional circle, constant \(J(x)=J_0\ne0\) has \(\partial_xJ=0\) and admits constant density. Zero-current implication therefore fails.

**Boundary conditions.** On a connected one-dimensional interval, \(\partial_xJ=0\) makes \(J\) constant with respect to \(x\) at each time. Adding zero current at one endpoint at every time and continuity to that boundary forces zero throughout. Zero current now follows jointly from stationary density, conservation, and the boundary condition.

This does not generalize to every higher-dimensional domain: circulation can have zero divergence and zero boundary-normal flux while remaining nonzero inside.

### Zero total current still need not mean every part is at rest

On a circle, two homogeneous material components can have densities \(\rho_0/2\) and velocities \(+u\) and \(-u\), with \(\rho_0>0,u\ne0\). Currents \(\rho_0u/2\) and \(-\rho_0u/2\) cancel, but both components move.

This is a two-component kinematic example, without conclusions about interactions or dynamical stability. For a medium genuinely described by one relation \(J=\rho v\), \(\rho>0\), \(J=0\) implies \(v=0\). That single constitutive relation must not be silently applied to mixtures or probability currents.

### Connection to quantum states on a circle

For a free model on a circle of length \(L>0\):

\[
\psi_n(x,t)=L^{-1/2}e^{i(k_nx-\omega_nt)},\qquad
k_n=\frac{2\pi n}{L},\quad
\omega_n=\frac{\hbar k_n^2}{2m}.
\]

With \(m>0,n\in\mathbb Z\), Foundation gives \(|\psi_n|^2=1/L\) and \(j_n=\hbar k_n/(mL)\). States \(n\) and \(-n\), for \(n\ne0\), have equal densities and opposite currents.

Position density cannot distinguish them; current direction does not factor through density alone, as P04 requires. This connects the quantum calculation to descriptive sufficiency without identifying probability current with classical material current.

## P12

**Stationary statistics do not require constant individual histories.**

**Probabilistic example premises.** Take \(A\ne0,\omega\ne0\), and \(\Theta\) uniform on \([0,2\pi)\). Define:

\[
X(t)=A\cos(\omega t+\Theta).
\]

“Strictly stationary” means the joint distribution at every finite time collection is invariant under shifting all times equally.

**Stationarity proof.** For \(t_1,\ldots,t_n\) and shift \(s\):

\[
(X(t_1+s),\ldots,X(t_n+s))
=\bigl(A\cos(\omega t_i+\Theta+\omega s)\bigr)_{i=1}^n.
\]

The variable \((\Theta+\omega s)\bmod2\pi\) remains uniform. The joint distribution is therefore that at \(t_1,\ldots,t_n\).

**Nonconstancy proof.** For every fixed phase, \(t\mapsto A\cos(\omega t+\Theta)\) is nonconstant on every nonempty open interval. Its derivative \(-A\omega\sin(\omega t+\Theta)\) is not identically zero there.

**Consequence.** Even invariance of every joint distribution under time translation differs from constancy of one realization. Constant one-time distributions are weaker still.

Uniform random phase is an example premise, not derived from the six foundations. This does not establish universally random motion, ergodicity under every temporal observation scheme, or exact observer knowledge of distributions.

## P13

**Instantaneous state equivalence does not guarantee unchanged evolution equations.**

**Additional model premises.** In the Schrödinger picture:

\[
i\hbar\partial_t\psi=H\psi,
\]

define \(\psi'(t)=e^{i\theta(t)}\psi(t)\), with differentiable real global phase. States and operators have domains making these differentiations and operations valid.

At each time, \(\psi'\) and \(\psi\) represent the same pure-state ray under [F-S09](../Foundation/Research/Sources.md#s09).

**Derivation.**

\[
i\hbar\partial_t\psi'
=-\hbar\dot\theta\,\psi'+H\psi'
=H'\psi',\qquad
H'=H-\hbar\dot\theta I.
\]

The global phase multiplies the identity, so commutation with \(H\) introduces no other terms.

**Conclusion.** Time-dependent representational changes require a corresponding generator transformation. A changing phase does not justify assuming \(\psi'\) obeys exactly the same \(H\). Constant phase makes the extra term zero.

This parallels extra terms for changing references in P01–P02, but shared differential form does not identify spatial bases with quantum phase physically.

## Several levels of constancy

P10 specifies when constant observables suffice for constant states. P11 exposes current information absent from density and boundary-condition effects. P12 separates probability laws from realizations. P13 separates ray equivalence from representational generator consistency.

No simple “more stationary means more at rest” ordering equates these. Sound conclusions name their object, reference, equivalence, and law structure.
